opus-5.5.text:
I think the question of "new homes" is really the right framing, because that's where the rubber meets the road. It's relatively easy to get a robot to do something well in the environment where you collected the data. The hard part is walking into a kitchen it has never seen, with a different countertop height, different lighting, a drawer handle it's never touched, and still doing the task.

So when I think about scaling laws there, I try to separate a few axes. One is the sheer amount of data, the number of hours or trajectories. Another is the diversity of environments, how many distinct homes or scenes you've collected in. A third is the diversity of objects and tasks within each environment. And then of course model size and compute. What you start to see is that these axes don't contribute equally. For generalization to a new home, environment diversity seems to matter a lot more than just piling up more demonstrations in the same few places. If you have a thousand hours in ten homes, that's often less useful than a few hundred hours spread across many more homes. There's a kind of diminishing return per environment: after a certain number of demos in one place, the marginal one teaches the model very little about the next place.

That has a really practical implication for how you design data collection. Instead of optimizing for throughput in a lab, you want cheap, portable ways to collect data in lots of real places, handheld devices, low-cost rigs, things people can bring into their own homes. The bottleneck shifts from "how many demos can we record" to "how many distinct worlds can we sample."

The other thing I'd say is that measuring this honestly is hard. In language models you have huge held-out text sets and the evaluation is cheap. In robotics, every evaluation in a new home is expensive, it's physical, it's noisy, success rates can swing a lot depending on small details. So part of exploring scaling laws is actually building the evaluation methodology: having truly held-out environments, enough trials to get meaningful error bars, and being disciplined about not tuning on your test homes. Otherwise you can fool yourself into seeing a nice curve that's really just overfitting to the evaluation set.

And I'd be a bit careful with the term "law." What we have so far are more like empirical trends in particular regimes. They're very useful for decision-making, like where to spend the next dollar of data collection, but I don't think we yet know whether they'll hold smoothly as we go up several orders of magnitude, or whether there are phase transitions where something like common sense about physical interaction suddenly emerges. That's one of the most exciting open questions to me.

r001.rationale: The response discusses environment diversity and generalization to new homes, but does not frame scaling as the number of training homes needed to reach a specified performance level.

r002.rationale: It describes diminishing returns from adding demonstrations within one environment. It does not suggest that adding more homes yields diminishing performance improvements on an unseen home.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the first thing to say is that "scaling law" means something a little different for robots than it does for language models. In language, you scale data and compute and you watch a loss curve go down smoothly. In robotics, the thing we actually care about is: you drop the robot into a house it has never seen, with a kitchen layout it has never seen, lighting it has never seen, a sponge of a different color, and does it still work? That's a question about distribution shift, not just about loss. So when I think about scaling laws for new homes, I'm really asking: as I add more training environments, more objects, more tasks, more embodiments, how does the success rate in a held-out home move? And is that curve predictable?

What we've found, and what a lot of the field has found, is that the axis that matters most is diversity, not raw volume. You can collect ten thousand hours in one apartment and it will barely help you in the apartment next door. But a few hundred hours spread across a hundred homes behaves very differently. The curve actually starts to look like a scaling law: roughly log-linear in the number of distinct environments. Every time you double the number of homes you've seen, you buy yourself a fairly consistent bump in new-home performance. That regularity is exciting, because it means we can start making forecasts. We can say, "To hit ninety percent on this task in an unseen kitchen, we probably need to see on the order of this many kitchens," and then go plan data collection around that number instead of guessing.

The second axis is the quality and structure of the data, which is where it gets messy. Human teleoperation data is expensive, so people are leaning on simulation, on video of humans, on cross-embodiment data from other robots. Each of those has its own scaling behavior and its own ceiling. Simulation scales almost for free in quantity, but there's a sim-to-real gap that you have to close with real data, and the amount of real data you need seems to go down as the sim diversity goes up. Human video gives you enormous coverage of homes and objects, but you're missing the action labels, so it mostly helps your visual representations and your sense of what tasks look like, not your low-level control. So in practice we're studying a kind of multi-source scaling law: what's the exchange rate between a sim episode, a human video clip, and a real teleop episode, in terms of new-home success? Having that exchange rate is what lets you allocate budget rationally.

And then there's the piece that I think people underrate, which is that the model has to actually be able to absorb the diversity. If your policy is small, you add more homes and the curve flattens early. Once you have a big pretrained vision-language backbone underneath the policy, the same data keeps paying off much longer. So model scale and data diversity are coupled, just like in LLMs, and you have to scale them together or you get misleading conclusions.

The honest caveat is that our curves are still noisy. Evaluating in real homes is slow, it's hard to get statistically clean numbers, and a lot of published "generalization" results are on a handful of environments. So I treat these as early scaling laws. But the direction is clear: new-home performance is predictable enough to plan around, and the bottleneck is building the data engine that can touch thousands of real homes, not inventing some new algorithm. That's the bet I'm making.

r001.rationale: The response says we can estimate how many kitchens are needed to reach 90% success on a task in an unseen kitchen, based on training across distinct homes.

r002.rationale: It says that with a small policy, adding more homes can make the performance curve flatten early, indicating diminishing gains in unseen-home performance.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking what we want to scale, and what we mean by performance. For a robot in a new home, the interesting question is whether it can do useful tasks reliably with very little adaptation. Can it find an object, pick it up, and put it away when the layout, lighting, and furniture are different from anything it has seen before?

Then I’d vary the amount and diversity of training experience separately. A thousand hours in one home might teach you something very different from a thousand hours spread across a hundred homes. You want to know whether improvement comes from more repetitions or from exposure to genuinely different environments.

The evaluation needs to happen in homes held out from training, and I’d measure more than average task success. How often does a person need to intervene? Can the robot recover when something goes wrong? How much experience in that new home does it need before it becomes useful?

I wouldn’t assume we already have a clean scaling law. I’d treat that as the empirical question. If performance improves predictably with broader experience, that gives us a way to decide what data to collect next. If it plateaus, we need to understand whether the bottleneck is perception, physical control, or the ability to recover over a long task.

r001.rationale: The response compares training in one home with training across many homes and proposes testing in held-out homes, but it does not frame the question as how many homes are needed to reach a specified performance level in a new home.

r002.rationale: It says performance might plateau, but does not specifically suggest that adding homes to the training data may produce diminishing improvements in unseen-home performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to treat performance in a new home as the thing we actually want to scale. A robot can get very good in the homes where it was trained and still struggle when the furniture moves, the lighting changes, or a drawer opens differently.

So I’d start with a set of held-out homes and measure how success changes as we increase training data, model size, and compute. But I’d also vary the number and diversity of training homes. Does collecting another thousand demonstrations in one kitchen help as much as collecting demonstrations across ten different kitchens? That’s an important distinction.

And I’d measure both out-of-the-box success and how much experience the robot needs to adapt. If it fails initially but learns a new home from a few interactions, that’s meaningful progress. The goal would be to find predictable relationships that tell us where to invest next: more demonstrations, more diverse environments, or better methods for adaptation.

r001.rationale: The response varies the number and diversity of training homes and measures performance in held-out homes, but does not frame the question as how many training homes are needed to reach a specified performance level.

r002.rationale: It compares more data from one kitchen with data across ten kitchens, but does not suggest that performance improvements from adding homes diminish.
